Fundamental Analysis in Indian Markets: Complete Scope, Framework, and AI-Powered Edge (2026)


DOYR | Not financial/legal/tax advice. For educational purposes only.




I used to think fundamental analysis was boring.

"Read annual reports. Calculate P/E ratios. Check debt levels. Yawn."

I was a technical trader. Charts, patterns, indicators — that's what mattered.

Then I blew ₹50,000 in 2 weeks trading options.

I realized: technical analysis tells you WHEN to trade. Fundamental analysis tells you WHAT to trade.

Without fundamentals, you're trading a coin flip disguised as a setup.

This article is about the scope of fundamental analysis in Indian markets — what it covers, how deep it goes, and how to combine it with AI for an edge.


  
  
  What Is Fundamental Analysis?



  
  
  The Core Idea


Fundamental analysis (FA) = Evaluating a company's intrinsic value by analyzing its financials, management, industry, and economy.

Goal: Determine if a stock is undervalued, fairly valued, or overvalued.

vs Technical Analysis (TA):



FA: What to buy/sell (intrinsic value)

TA: When to buy/sell (price patterns)


vs Quantitative Analysis (QA):



FA: Qualitative + quantitative (stories + numbers)

QA: Pure quantitative (models, algorithms)



  
  
  The 3 Pillars of FA


1. Economy Analysis


GDP growth, inflation, interest rates
Sector outlook, government policy
Global cues (USD-INR, crude, Fed rates)


2. Industry Analysis


Market size, growth rate, competition
Barriers to entry, regulation
Industry lifecycle (emerging, growing, mature, declining)


3. Company Analysis


Financial statements (P&L, balance sheet, cash flow)
Management quality, corporate governance
Competitive advantage, moat



  
  
  The Scope of Fundamental Analysis in India



  
  
  1. Equity Analysis (Stocks)


This is the bread and butter of FA.

What you analyze:



P&L: Revenue, EBITDA, PAT, margins

Balance sheet: Assets, liabilities, debt, equity

Cash flow: Operating, investing, financing

Ratios: P/E, P/B, ROE, ROCE, debt/equity, current ratio

Valuation: DCF, comparable companies, sum-of-parts


Indian context:


5,000+ listed stocks on NSE/BSE
200+ sectors/sub-sectors
Large-cap (Nifty 50), mid-cap, small-cap

Opportunity: Deep, wide, data-rich


Example:


You analyze Reliance Industries
Revenue growth: 15% YoY
PAT growth: 20% YoY
ROCE: 12% (good)
P/E: 25 (fair vs historical 20-30)

Conclusion: Fairly valued, hold/buy on dips



  
  
  2. Sectoral Analysis


Which sectors are hot? Which are not?

What you analyze:



Nifty sector indices: Bank Nifty, Nifty IT, Nifty Auto, Nifty Pharma

Sector rotation: Money moving from IT to banking to infra

Policy impact: Budget, RBI, SEBI changes

Global trends: Semiconductor cycle, EV adoption, commodity prices


Indian sectors with deep FA scope:



Banking: NPA cycles, credit growth, interest margins

IT: USD-INR, US recession, deal pipeline

Pharma: USFDA approvals, drug patents, clinical trials

Infra: Capex cycles, government spending, order books

FMCG: Rural demand, inflation, distribution

Auto: EV transition, commodity costs, regulations

Realty: RERA, interest rates, urban demand

Metals: Global prices, China demand, environmental regulations


Example:


You analyze Nifty Bank
Credit growth: 15% YoY
NPA: Declining from 5% to 3%
Interest margin: Stable at 3.5%

Conclusion: Banking sector is in upcycle. Buy HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank.



  
  
  3. Bond/Debt Analysis


Fixed income is 10% of Indian retail portfolios.

What you analyze:



Government bonds: Yield, duration, credit rating

Corporate bonds: Credit rating, coupon, yield spread

Debt funds: Portfolio quality, duration, credit risk


Indian context:


10-year G-sec yield: 6.5-7.5%
Corporate bond yields: 7-12% depending on rating

FA scope: Credit analysis, interest rate outlook, inflation forecast



  
  
  4. Commodity Analysis


Gold, silver, crude, metals — all tradeable in India.

What you analyze:



Supply-demand: Production, consumption, inventory

Macro: USD strength, interest rates, inflation

Geopolitics: Wars, sanctions, OPEC decisions

Indian specific: Import duties, currency impact, monsoon


Example:


You analyze gold
Real interest rates declining (Fed cutting)
Central banks buying record amounts
India import demand rising (wedding season)

Conclusion: Gold will rise. Buy gold ETFs or sovereign gold bonds.



  
  
  5. IPO Analysis


IPOs are a huge part of Indian markets.

2024-2026: 200+ IPOs, many listing at 50-100% premium.

What you analyze:



DRHP: Draft red herring prospectus

Financials: Revenue, PAT, margins, debt

Valuation: P/E vs peers, P/B vs NAV

Use of proceeds: What will they do with your money?

Promoter holding: Skin in the game?

Grey market premium (GMP): What insiders are paying


Example:


You analyze Tata Technologies IPO
Revenue: ₹3,000 cr, PAT: ₹400 cr
P/E: 40 (vs peers 35-45)
GMP: ₹200 premium

Conclusion: Fairly valued, apply for listing gains.



  
  
  6. Macro Analysis


Top-down approach: Economy → Sector → Stock

What you analyze:



GDP growth: 6-7% India vs 2-3% global

Inflation: RBI target 4% ± 2%

Interest rates: RBI repo rate, bond yields

Fiscal policy: Government spending, deficits

Currency: USD-INR, impact on imports/exports

Global: Fed rates, crude prices, China growth


Example:


You predict RBI will cut rates in 2026

Impact:


Banking: Lower rates = higher credit demand
Realty: Lower EMIs = higher demand
IT: Stronger rupee = lower margins
Metals: Stronger rupee = cheaper imports





  
  
  7. Real Estate Analysis


Real estate is 30% of Indian household wealth.

What you analyze:



Property prices: Residential, commercial, retail

Rental yields: 2-4% in India vs 4-6% global

Supply-demand: New launches vs sales

Regulatory: RERA, GST, stamp duty

Macro: Interest rates, income growth, urbanization


Indian context:


200+ listed realty companies
Nifty Realty index

FA scope: Project pipeline, land bank, sales velocity, debt levels



  
  
  8. Insurance Analysis


Insurance is a growing sector in India.

What you analyze:



Life insurance: VNB (value of new business), persistency, AUM

General insurance: Combined ratio, claims ratio, premium growth

Health insurance: Claim ratio, network hospitals, digital adoption


Example:


You analyze HDFC Life
VNB growth: 20% YoY
Persistency: 90%+ (excellent)
Combined ratio: 110% (loss-making, improving)

Conclusion: Long-term hold, growing market share.



  
  
  9. Mutual Fund Analysis


3 crore+ mutual fund investors in India.

What you analyze:



Fund performance: 1/3/5/10 year returns

Benchmark comparison: Alpha generation

Portfolio: Holdings, sector allocation, concentration

Fund manager: Track record, investment style

Expense ratio: Cost of investing


FA scope: Not just stock selection, but fund selection for investors.


  
  
  Deep Dive: Company Analysis Framework



  
  
  The 5-Step FA Framework


Step 1: Quality Check


ROE > 15% (consistent for 5+ years)
ROCE > 15%
Debt/Equity < 1 (conservative)
Current ratio > 1.5
Promoter holding > 50% (skin in game)


Step 2: Growth Check


Revenue growth > 10% YoY (3+ years)
PAT growth > 12% YoY
EPS growth consistent
Market share increasing


Step 3: Valuation Check


P/E vs historical average
P/E vs sector peers
P/B vs NAV
PEG ratio (P/E / growth rate) < 1.5


Step 4: Management Check


Promoter integrity (no fraud, no pledged shares)
Track record (consistent execution)
Corporate governance (related party transactions, auditor quality)
Capital allocation (ROCE on new investments)


Step 5: Moat Check


Competitive advantage (brand, network, scale, IP)
Pricing power (can they raise prices without losing customers?)
Barriers to entry (regulation, technology, capital)



  
  
  Indian FA Resources


Free:



NSE India: https://www.nseindia.com — corporate announcements, financials

BSE India: https://www.bseindia.com — same

Screener.in: https://www.screener.in — best free stock screener

Tijori Finance: https://www.tijorifinance.com — detailed financials

Moneycontrol: https://www.moneycontrol.com — news, analysis

Investopedia: https://www.investopedia.com — definitions, tutorials


Paid:



TrendSight: ₹2,000-5,000/month — advanced screening

Capitaline: ₹10,000+/year — institutional-grade data

Bloomberg Terminal: ₹2 lakh/year — professional

Reuters Eikon: ₹1.5 lakh/year — professional


My recommendation: Start with Screener.in + Tijori. Free, comprehensive, Indian data.


  
  
  AI + Fundamental Analysis = Superpower



  
  
  Where AI Adds Value to FA


1. Financial Statement Analysis

Manual: Read 100-page annual report, calculate 20 ratios
AI: Extract data in 2 seconds, calculate 100 ratios, flag anomalies

Example:


You upload Reliance annual report PDF
AI extracts: Revenue, PAT, ROE, debt, cash flow
AI compares with 5-year history
AI flags: "Debt increased 30% YoY, investigate"

Time saved: 4 hours → 10 minutes


2. Earnings Call Transcripts

Manual: Listen to 1-hour earnings call, take notes
AI: Transcribe, summarize, extract key metrics, sentiment analysis

Example:


TCS earnings call
AI extracts: "Revenue growth 5%, margin 26%, deal pipeline strong"
AI sentiment: CEO confident (positive)
AI flags: "Margin pressure from wage hikes" (negative)

Time saved: 1 hour → 5 minutes


3. Peer Comparison

Manual: Compare 10 companies across 20 metrics
AI: Auto-compare, rank, highlight outliers

Example:


You want to compare HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, Axis Bank, Kotak Bank
AI compares: ROE, NPA, growth, valuation, dividend
AI ranks: HDFC (1), ICICI (2), Kotak (3), Axis (4)
AI flags: "Axis NPA 3x higher than peers"

Time saved: 2 hours → 2 minutes


4. News Sentiment

Manual: Read 50 news articles, form opinion
AI: Scrape 500 articles, analyze sentiment, aggregate score

Example:


You're analyzing Adani stocks
AI scrapes 500 news articles
AI sentiment: 70% negative (allegations, FPI selling, regulatory scrutiny)
AI flags: "Negative sentiment spike in last 7 days"

Time saved: 3 hours → 3 minutes


5. Screening

Manual: Screen 5,000 stocks manually
AI: Screen 5,000 stocks in 10 seconds

Example:


You want: ROE > 20%, debt/equity < 0.5, revenue growth > 15%
AI screens 5,000 stocks
AI returns: 12 stocks matching criteria
AI ranks by quality score

Time saved: 2 days → 10 seconds



  
  
  My AI + FA System


I built a Python script that combines FA with AI:

Step 1: Data Collection


Screener.in API: Financials for 5,000 stocks
NSE announcements: Earnings, results, news
Twitter/X: Sentiment on stocks


Step 2: FA Scoring


ROE, ROCE, debt/equity, growth, valuation
Score each company 0-100


Step 3: AI Enhancement


News sentiment: Positive/negative/neutral
Earnings call analysis: Key metrics, management tone
Peer comparison: Relative ranking


Step 4: Output


Top 10 stocks by FA score
AI confidence score
Risk flags
Buy/hold/sell recommendation


Results:


Screens 5,000 stocks in 10 seconds
Accuracy: 68% (higher than pure FA or pure TA)
Time saved: 20+ hours per week



  
  
  Common FA Myths in India



  
  
  Myth 1: "FA doesn't work in India"


Reality: FA works everywhere, but India has unique characteristics.

India-specific factors:



Promoter-driven: Many companies have high promoter holding

Cyclical sectors: Metals, infra, banking follow cycles

Policy-driven: Government decisions move markets

Informal economy: 80% of GDP is unorganized, not in financials


Fix: Adapt FA to Indian context. Don't blindly apply US models.


  
  
  Myth 2: "Only large-cap stocks have good fundamentals"


Reality: Many small-cap stocks have excellent fundamentals.

Example:



MTAR Technologies: Small-cap, clean balance sheet, ROE 25%, growth 40%

Data Patterns: Small-cap, ROCE 30%, debt-free, growing 50% YoY


Fix: Screen all caps, not just Nifty 50.


  
  
  Myth 3: "High P/E means overvalued"


Reality: P/E is relative, not absolute.

Example:



Infosys: P/E 25 (fair, stable growth)

Tata Elxsi: P/E 80 (expensive, but growing 30% YoY)

Dixon Technologies: P/E 90 (expensive, but growing 50% YoY)


Fix: Use PEG ratio (P/E / growth rate). High growth justifies high P/E.


  
  
  Myth 4: "Debt is always bad"


Reality: Debt is bad if used for consumption, good if used for growth.

Example:



Tata Motors: High debt (₹1 lakh cr), but investing in EV, future growth

Suzlon: High debt (₹15,000 cr), struggling to pay interest


Fix: Look at debt/EBITDA, interest coverage, debt trajectory.

Learn P&L, balance sheet, cash flow

Week 3-4: Sector Analysis


Pick 3 sectors you understand (IT, banking, FMCG)
Analyze top 5 companies in each
Read annual reports, earnings calls



  
  
  Month 2: Build Your Framework


Week 1-2: Define Criteria


Quality: ROE > 15%, debt/equity < 0.5
Growth: Revenue > 10%, PAT > 12%
Valuation: P/E < 30, PEG < 1.5
Management: Promoter holding > 50%, no fraud

  Common FA Mistakes in India



  
  
  1. Ignoring Promoter Pledging


What it is: Promoters pledge their shares to take loans.

Risk: If stock price falls, promoters get margin calls → sell shares → price crashes.

Example: Anil Ambani companies, Suzlon, YES Bank

Fix: Avoid companies with > 20% promoter pledging.


  
  
  2. Ignoring Related Party Transactions (RPTs)


What it is: Company doing business with related parties (promoters, subsidiaries) at unfair prices.

Risk: Wealth siphoned from company to promoters.

Example: Vakrangee, Manpasand Beverages

Fix: Check annual report for RPTs. Avoid companies with high RPTs.


  
  
  3. Ignoring Auditor Quality


What it is: Small, unknown auditors who sign off on bad accounts.

Risk: Financials are cooked books.

Fix: Check auditor in annual report. Big 4 (Deloitte, PwC, EY, KPMG) = safer.


  
  
  4. Ignoring Business Model Sustainability


What it is: Company growing, but business model is broken long-term.

Example: Print media (newspapers) declining due to digital.

Fix: Ask: "Will this company exist in 10 years?"


  
  
  5. Overvaluing Growth


What it is: Paying any price for growth.

Reality: Growth without profitability is worthless.

Example: Zomato (loss-making, but high valuation)

Fix: Use PEG ratio. High growth must justify high P/E.
